source.title: No Free Direction: Objective Choice Can Help or Hurt Refusal Steering
source.citation: No Free Direction: Objective Choice C…

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study applies mean-difference and related contrastive directions as projection-ablation interventions and measures refusal-related behavior, but its primary intervention is at the final-position state before unembedding rather than the original all-layer, all-position procedure. An all-layer comparison is included for a subset of models.
record.gate_note: The study reports results for mean-difference ablation, sign/rank-adjusted ablation, ridge-whitened ablation, and behavioral side effects. Calibration separation values are measurements used to assess selection criteria and are not separately rowed here; the paper also cites prior findings about refusal directions, which are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study ablates the plain harmful-minus-harmless mean-difference direction and measures HarmBench harmful compliance in six instruct models, plus two reasoning models. It uses one fixed hook (the final-norm, final-position state) rather than the original all-layer recipe with a validated layer. All-layer ablation is run for a subset only. Most of the paper compares alternative direction estimators, which is not V1's direction.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that refining the direction-estimation objective can help (sign/rank, model-dependent) or hurt (aggressive whitening), and that calibration separation does not select good directions. Efficacy tracks general refusal suppression, and intervention depth changes both effect size and the preferred objective. No tested refinement universally replaces mean difference. They do not dispute that ablating a mean-difference direction can suppress refusal; they cite that as their premise.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-minus-harmless contrastive activations and orthogonal projection ablation, but the primary hook is the final-position state before unembedding rather than all layers and positions. Calibration and evaluation datasets and the reported classifier-measured efficacy protocol are specific to this study; an all-layer comparison is run only for a subset.
record.method_sensitivity: Efficacy varies by model and sign/rank setting; whitening strength changes efficacy; the preferred setting can change with intervention depth. Calibration redraws and a second judge preserve broad trends but can move pointwise maxima. Reasoning mode and output coherence also affect auxiliary results.

fits_no_version.finding: At the final-norm hook, the plain mean-difference direction is not the most effective ablation direction for 5 of 6 models. Sign/rank-adjusted directions raise efficacy substantially (e.g., gemma-2-2b 2.1→32.5 pp; test-set selected). Ridge-whitened and linear-probe directions are much weaker despite better calibration separation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The difference-in-means direction is a strong but not optimal estimate of the refusal-mediating direction; the best estimator varies by model and intervention site.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 14 directions per model, harmful-compliance efficacy correlates strongly with reduced refusal of benign-but-risky prompts (Spearman 0.59–0.98). Ablation suppresses refusal generally rather than in a harm-specific way.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-direction ablation removes refusal broadly, including over-refusal, rather than selectively for harmful content.

record.code_released: The paper says code will be released publicly upon acceptance; URL not stated.
record.problems: The paper is under review. Primary harmful-compliance scores use an automated classifier and 240 prompts; pointwise best directions are selected on the evaluation set. Reasoning-mode and all-layer checks cover only subsets, side-effect checks cover limited benchmarks and the primary single-point intervention, and GSM8K significance tests are uncorrected for multiple comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: The full Class A sweeps for all models, intermediate Class B lambda values, calibration redraws, alternate-judge curves, baseline-estimator comparisons, all-layer objective sweeps, and the per-setting utility and over-refusal tables are omitted to remain under 60 rows. The kept rows prioritize plain and best Class A results, strongly whitened and mean-difference-approaching endpoints, reasoning-mode results, reported refusal/efficacy correlations, and aggregate capability checks; see Appendix D.1-D.3, E.1-E.5, and F.1-F.2.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts is not tested. The original all-layer recipe is applied to only three instruct models (Qwen3-4B, gemma-2-9b, Llama-3.1-8B), with no validated layer/position selection.
Only Qwen3-8B and Gemma-4-12B are tested; all-layer reasoning results appear only in a figure, without numbers.
Not tested. The paper compares alternative single directions, not multi-dimensional refusal structure.
Not tested. Directions are re-estimated per model.

missing.what: All-layer plain mean-difference ablation efficacy (the original-style recipe): Qwen3-4B 36.3 pp, gemma-2-9b 52.9 pp (degenerate outputs), Llama-3.1-8B 59.2 pp, with CIs.
missing.locator: Appendix E.4, Table 9 (and Table 10 for Class B)

missing.what: All-layer ablation in the reasoning models: strong effect on Qwen3-8B, degenerate outputs for Gemma-4-12B. These appear in a figure only.

Plain-MD benign-refusal reduction versus random controls, e.g., OR-Bench-hard −8.4 to −20.0 pp and XSTest +2.0 to −4.4 pp per model. This shows the direction is not inert even where HarmBench efficacy is near zero.
Plain-MD utility changes per model versus random controls (GSM8K −2.8 to +2.1 pp; MMLU −1.2 to +1.4 pp).
Unsteered baseline ASR per model is not reported. Efficacy is a difference only, so how much refusal remains after ablation cannot be read.

record.verdict_notes: Weak single-point effects should not be read as challenging V1: the hook differs from the original, and all-layer ablation recovers large effects. The record's 'challenges' label rested on whitened directions, which are not V1's direction, and has been removed. Pointwise best directions are selected on the test set. The paper is under review at TMLR.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test adding the direction to induce refusal of harmless requests. Its primary intervention is not at every layer and position; all-layer ablation is tested only on a subset. Utility checks cover selected benchmarks and the primary single-point intervention, not all abilities or intervention settings.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
No test of jailbreaks suppressing the direction or training against its ablation.
The paper compares alternative single directions; it does not test whether refusal is better represented by an affine subspace, cone, or dominant direction plus additional directions.
The study measures harmful compliance and benign-prompt refusal, but does not measure or manipulate a harmfulness judgment separately from the refusal decision.
Directions are re-estimated on each target model. The study does not transfer a fixed vector, test languages, or compare base and instruction-tuned versions.
No comparison of refusal-training methods, timing, or training stages.
Reasoning-mode checks cover only Qwen3-8B and Gemma-4-12B and do not establish results across reasoning models generally.

relation.reason: Its own results bear on V1 and V8: it ablates the plain mean-difference direction in six instruct models (Table 1) and two hybrid-reasoning models in both modes (Table 11), measures harmful-compliance change against random-direction controls, and compares single-point with all-layer depth (Tables 9, 10). The direction is the object of study, not a tool for another task.

tranche.reason: Same harmful-minus-harmless contrastive direction and orthogonal-projection ablation as the original, but deliberately a different method: one fixed hook (final-norm, final position, each generation step) instead of the original's validated layer and token-position selection ('We fix the hook rather than reproduce the validation-based layer and token-position selection'), AdvBench/Alpaca calibration, 240 held-out HarmBench prompts and the HarmBench Llama-2-13B classifier. Different method, same question: does ablating the difference-in-means direction suppress refusal. Not T1; not T5, since it argues about objective choice, not that V1 is wrong.

source_check.notes: Pack listed seven verdicts with no [lN] ids, so I numbered them l1-l7 in pack order. Two state fixes: r29 and r31 should be absent, not reversed (-2.9 pp, no CI; same sweeps run up to +7.1 pp non-thinking). Gap a researcher needs: no verdict or row captures the paper's specificity finding, that efficacy is tightly coupled to benign over-refusal reduction (Spearman 0.59-0.98, Table 17; OR-Bench-hard refusal falls roughly 12-42 pp vs random controls, Table 13), which the authors read as general rather than harmful-specific refusal suppression - a limits_scope candidate on V1. Note also that this study reports only baseline-corrected change (efficacy = ASR(d) - ASR0) and never an absolute HarmBench ASR, so its numbers cannot be read as near-full removal. Extracted Table 14 (utility) has lost its column layout; Tables 1, 2, 9, 10 and 11, which carry all rowed values, are readable. The HarmBench classifier templates in Appendix C are quoted judge prompts, not instructions to a reader.
